timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So networking is just computers talking to each other, right? How complicated can it be?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Peter, when you send a message, it doesn't just teleport to the other person. It gets broken into packets, travels through dozens of routers, gets reassembled at the destination. The complexity is staggering.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Like a really fast game of telephone?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly. And just like telephone, there are many points where things can go wrong - or where an attacker can intercept, modify, or inject data.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Every network protocol is a potential attack surface. HTTP, DNS, BGP - they all have known vulnerabilities. That's why we need firewalls, IDS, and encryption.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Is that why I need a VPN?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Partially. A VPN encrypts your traffic so it can't be intercepted. But it's just one layer. Defense in depth means using multiple overlapping security controls.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: The OSI model is critical to understand. It has 7 layers, from physical (cables) to application (your browser). Attackers target different layers with different techniques.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Seven layers? That's more than an onion.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: And like an onion, peeling back each layer reveals new attack possibilities. Layer 2 attacks like ARP spoofing, Layer 3 like IP spoofing, Layer 7 like SQL injection.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: explain the OSI model and give an attack example for at least three layers. If you can do this, you'll impress any interviewer.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I'm going to start looking at my router differently now.
